papers.title: Real-time detection of N2 and N3 sleep from scalp and intracranial EEG
papers.abstract: Sleep rhythms such as slow oscillations and spindles arise predominantly during N2 and N3 sleep (N2+N3). Closed-loop stimulation targeting these rhythms is a promising strategy to enhance memory. Such stimulation requires online sleep stage classification. Conventional staging labels completed 30-s epochs using past and future data and cannot support online staging. We developed a causal tracker that, every 2 s, estimates the current stage from the preceding 10 s of scalp or intracranial EEG. We also evaluated a simulated rule that permits stimulation after three consecutive estimates indicating N2+N3 sleep. In six adults with drug-resistant epilepsy with simultaneous scalp EEG and stereo-EEG, real-time N2+N3 discrimination remained close to offline scoring of the same recordings (scalp AUC 0.953 versus 0.958). Thalamic channels alone reached AUC 0.934 and exceeded mesial temporal channels in every patient, and scalp plus thalamus performed best (0.967). The scalp tracker, retrained in 28 healthy adults, reached 0.976. When patients transitioned into N2+N3 sleep with stimulation initially disabled, the rule permitted stimulation within 5 min in 63-73% of transitions, with a median delay of 42-64 s among those detected. After leaving N2+N3, stimulation was disabled after a median of 19-22 s. The rule also switched on incorrectly 1.4-1.8 times per hour outside N2+N3 and remained active during 28-31% of REM in patients, compared with 2% in healthy adults. These findings show that both scalp and thalamic EEG can support real-time N2+N3 detection and inform when stimulation is permitted. Translationally, implanted thalamic leads, increasingly used for neuromodulation in epilepsy, could support sleep-stage-dependent stimulation without scalp EEG, while scalp EEG might be used for noninvasive neuromodulation. Closed-loop systems should be evaluated not only by sleep-stage classification accuracy but also by how reliably and promptly they enable and disable stimulation.

papers.title: Automated Sleep Staging Performance Across Two Experimental Sleep Manipulation Protocols in Adolescents.
papers.abstract: Automated sleep staging algorithms improve the scalability of polysomnography analysis in adolescent research but are primarily validated in undisturbed, single-night sleep recordings. It remains unclear whether these algorithms maintain performance when sleep architecture is experimentally manipulated. This study evaluated the validity of two popular automated sleep staging approaches across two distinct sleep manipulation paradigms in adolescents: a sleep restriction protocol (N=43, mean age [SD]=13.37[1.06] years; four nights including two sleep extension [10hr] and two restriction [4hr] nights) and a slow-wave sleep deprivation (SWSD) protocol (N=18, mean age [SD]=17.17[1.79] years; baseline, SWSD, and recovery nights). Automated sleep staging was performed using the POPulation-level Sleep Stager (POPS), the Yet Another Spindle Algorithm (YASA), and combined POPS+YASA. Manual polysomnography scoring by experienced sleep technicians served as the reference standard. Agreement was assessed using Cohen's κ, and stage-specific performance was evaluated using F1 scores and confusion matrices. Mixed-effects models tested differences in overall and stage-specific agreement across nights. All staging approaches demonstrated moderate-to-substantial agreement with manual scoring across manipulated sleep conditions (κ range=0.53-0.76). In the sleep restriction study, agreement was lower in restricted versus extended sleep (P<0.05), and agreement declined across restriction nights, with poorer Wake, N1, and N2 classification, while N3 remained preserved. In the SWSD study, overall agreement was lower on the SWSD night, with poorer N3 classification while other stages were preserved. Automated sleep staging performance may be less consistent in adolescents when sleep is curtailed or fragmented; future studies should develop and validate these algorithms under multiple sleep conditions.

papers.title: Sleep-like slow waves in wakefulness index post-stroke behavioural alterations.
papers.abstract: Increases in high-amplitude, low-frequency EEG oscillations during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep serve as markers of neuronal silencing, which disrupts functional connectivity and is associated with a loss of awareness and responsiveness. Cortical slowing likewise occurs during wakefulness, upon sleep deprivation, and accompanies performance deterioration. Recent work has revealed similar oscillations (termed 'sleep-like slow waves') following stroke in brain regions close or connected to a brain lesion, offering a plausible but untested mechanism for stroke-related behavioural impairment. Here, we simultaneously recorded EEG and behavioural performance while 30 unilateral stroke patients (12 left hemisphere, 18 right hemisphere) and 27 age-matched healthy adults completed a computerised perceptual decision-making task. Stroke patients had predominantly middle cerebral artery strokes (n=25), with a small subset of posterior cerebral artery (n=4), and anterior cerebral artery/middle cerebral artery (n=1) lesions. Sleep-like slow waves occurred more frequently in stroke patients relative to healthy controls, with limited spatial specificity when comparing patients with left and right lesion sites (more slow waves ipsilateral of the lesion). Furthermore, there was a significant correlation between slow wave occurrence and the accuracy and speed of perceptual reports in stroke patients, suggesting that variations in the occurrence of slow waves may contribute to cognitive heterogeneity post-stroke. As sleep-like slow waves predict deficits in perceptual decision-making following stroke, they represent a plausible mechanism of post-lesion functional network dysfunction extending beyond the damaged regions, thereby contributing to broader cognitive impairments.

papers.title: Detection of Spreading Depolarization with Noninvasive Electroencephalography.
papers.abstract: Spreading depolarizations (SDs) are waves of near-complete breakdown of the transmembrane ion gradients that underlie migraine aura and occur in patients with moderate-to-severe traumatic, ischemic or hemorrhagic brain injury. SDs are involved in primary and secondary brain injury. They are associated with poor neurological outcome and represent a modifiable therapeutic target. However, despite decades of investigation, SD detection still requires invasive subdural electrocorticography (ECoG) using an implanted subdural electrode strip, restricting monitoring to a small subset of neurosurgical patients. We developed WAVEFRONT, a noninvasive scalp electroencephalography (EEG) biomarker of SD based on spatiotemporal propagation characteristics of delta-band EEG activity. The biomarker was trained and validated using concurrent, multi-day scalp EEG and invasive subdural electrocorticography recordings from patients with traumatic brain injury (TBI), subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), or malignant hemispheric stroke (MHS) across three institutions. We assessed out-of-sample performance across institutions, diagnosis, and surgical approaches, as well as calibration, temporal synchrony, and spatial specificity relative to gold-standard SDs annotated on ECoG. Clinical utility was further evaluated in 607 patients comatose after cardiac arrest from the multicenter International Cardiac Arrest REsearch (I-CARE) consortium, a population in whom invasive monitoring is not performed. Outcome analyses excluded patients who died (Cerebral Performance Category [CPC] 5) because death may reflect decisions to withdraw life-sustaining treatment in addition to neurological injury. A total of 1,119 gold-standard SDs were annotated in 32 patients (TBI, n=17; SAH, n=12; MHS, n=3; range 0-187 SDs per patient). Across exhaustive cross-validation and institution-, diagnosis-, and surgical approach-based hold-out analyses, WAVEFRONT models trained on one set of patients consistently maintained high performance when evaluated in previously unseen out-of-group cohorts. At the optimal operating point, WAVEFRONT achieved a mean cross-validated true positive rate of 97.3±1% with a false positive rate of 6.0±0.5%, calculated over 2-min sliding windows with 30-s overlaps. The cumulative duration of WAVEFRONT detections within 30-hour windows strongly correlated with the number of SDs measured by invasive ECoG (R 2 =0.7411). Scalp-detected depressions were spatially consistent with the location of the invasive recording strip, and visual inspection demonstrated close temporal correspondence with invasive detections, including during SD clusters. External validation in the independent I-CARE cohort using WAVEFRONT trained on the invasive-monitoring cohort demonstrated significantly greater SD burden on day 3 of post-arrest EEG monitoring among patients with poor neurological outcome (CPC 3-4, n=29) than those with good outcome (CPC 1-2, n=225; p=0.007). Eight decades after Leão's description of SD in 1944, we propose and validate a noninvasive scalp EEG biomarker of SD. Consistent performance across institution-, diagnosis-, and surgical approach-based hold-out analyses, together with burden calibration, spatial specificity, and temporal synchrony with ECoG detections, supports the validity of the WAVEFRONT framework. The association of biomarker burden with neurologic outcome after cardiac arrest suggests that noninvasive monitoring may enable investigation of spreading depolarizations in populations where invasive monitoring is not feasible. Future studies should evaluate prospective performance, treatment responsiveness, and disease-specific associations of the SD biomarker with clinical outcome.

papers.title: Probing EEG Foundation Model Attention Maps for Lightweight Interpretable Emotion Recognition
papers.abstract: Foundation Models (FMs) trained on EEG signals promise subject- and dataset-independent pipelines for brain-computer interface (BCI) applications, but have yet to consistently outperform task-specific architectures, and their large representations are costly to compute and store. As a means of advancing the understanding of the Foundation Models' inner mechanisms, we propose a lightweight alternative that exploits the self-attention mechanism of REVE, a pretrained EEG FM, to derive features similar to weighted Functional Connectivity (FC) without any fine-tuning. Inspired by kernel-based FC matrices, we aggregate the raw first-layer attention weights of a single head over the full duration of dataset trials into weighted channel-to-channel adjacency matrices. These matrices replace standard encoder representation vectors as classification features, substantially reducing computational cost. We further introduce a label-free, symmetry-based criterion, motivated by the emergence of near-symmetric attention patterns in trained encoder-decoder transformers, ranking attention heads by how much discriminative information they carry. Classical machine learning classifiers are then trained on the single most informative head's attention-derived FC matrix and achieve balanced accuracy and F1 scores on the SEED-IV emotion-recognition dataset that are competitive with several fully fine-tuned state-of-the-art EEG Foundation Models, requiring at least two orders of magnitude fewer calculations than the standard use of the encoder. Subsequent cortical region analysis revealed a significant over-representation of frontal region connections by ranking the most discriminative FC matrix connectivity edges, validating our methods as consistent with prior affective-computing literature. These results suggest that interpretable, computationally inexpensive linear probing of attention maps is a viable route to deploying EEG Foundation Models in resource-constrained settings.

Classifiers on the single best head achieved balanced accuracy and F1 competitive with several fully fine-tuned EEG foundation models on SEED-IV with at least two orders of magnitude fewer computations, and highlighted over-represented frontal connections.

papers.title: Next generation Human Neocortical Neurosolver model with biophysically realistic somatic, dendritic and synaptic dynamics
papers.abstract: The Human Neocortical Neurosolver (HNN) is an open-source biophysical modeling tool for multiscale interpretation of human electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) signals. HNN's foundation is a pre-tuned canonical neocortical circuit model consisting of excitatory pyramidal neurons and inhibitory interneurons in supra- (L2/3) and infragranular (L5) layers. This model was originally developed based on studies in rodent and non-human primate cortices when dynamics of human neurons were poorly characterized. Yet recent advances in recordings from human tissue now provide unprecedented detail to update the model. Here, we present a significantly updated model for use in the HNN software, with electrophysiological properties and synaptic connections tuned to human tissue. Beyond reproducing biologically realistic somatic dynamics, the pyramidal cells simulate dendritic calcium (Ca2+) spikes in the L5 extratelencephalic-projecting (ET) neurons, and shorter dendritic spikes in the L2/3 pyramidal neurons. We demonstrate how the updated circuitry and new features in the HNN software can be used to disentangle somatic, synaptic, and dendritic contributions to human E-/MEG signatures. The model is distributed with workflows to simulate event-related responses and oscillations, and tutorials demonstrating how membrane potentials, Ca2+ dynamics, and synaptic currents can be recorded and visualized. These enhancements allow extensive model validations based on in vitro and in vivo electrophysiology, voltage and Ca2+ imaging, and provide users with novel insights on the mechanisms underlying E-/MEG signals.

papers.title: EEG-based deep learning estimates preterm infants' cerebral age: Contribution of slow-wave and cross-frequency coupling.
papers.abstract: Reliably estimating cerebral maturation in preterm newborns is crucial for early identification of atypical neurodevelopment. We developed a deep-learning framework using a convolutional neural network (CNN) to predict postmenstrual age (PMA) from spontaneous neural activity in EEG recordings of 165 healthy preterm infants (28-38 weeks PMA). The model achieved a mean absolute error of 0.75 ± 0.60 weeks, with 73.9% of prediction errors within one week. To identify key neurophysiological drivers, we systematically manipulated signal components. Results showed that removing low-frequency activity (<4 Hz) significantly degraded performance and disrupting phase-amplitude coupling selectively impaired prediction accuracy before 34 weeks PMA, while high-frequency activity (>12 Hz) had minimal impact. Our results demonstrate that maturation signatures are primarily driven by slow-wave dynamics and their hierarchical coupling with faster oscillations, which are fundamental hallmarks of early neurodevelopment.

papers.title: Expectation-driven gain modulation of preparatory spatial attention.
papers.abstract: The visual system can flexibly adjust attentional deployment to match task demands, but whether observers can proactively modulate the spatial scope of attention based on expectations about upcoming search difficulty remains unclear. According to the zoom lens model, attention can narrow or broaden its spatial extent, with narrower focus enhancing processing efficiency, a mechanism that would benefit target discrimination in crowded displays. We tested whether observers adjust attentional scope when expecting sparse versus dense search arrays by combining spatial cueing with block-wise manipulations of display density expectations. Participants performed a visual search task in which endogenous cues predicted target location, while blocks predominantly contained either sparse (1 target, 3 distractors) or dense (1 target, 7 distractors) displays. We applied inverted encoding models to broadband EEG data to reconstruct spatial channel tuning functions, enabling precise characterization of both the locus and breadth of attentional deployment. Behaviorally, expecting difficult searches selectively improved accuracy at cued locations without costs elsewhere. Consistent with this selective benefit, neural measurements revealed that expectancy enhanced the amplitude of spatially selective responses at the attended location but did not alter tuning width. These findings demonstrate that expectations about search difficulty modulate attention through gain-based signal enhancement rather than adjustments to spatial scope, revealing that preparatory attentional control operates via amplitude modulation within a stable spatial focus. This mechanism complements reactive attentional adjustments and provides an efficient means for the visual system to optimize processing under predictable task demands.

papers.title: Electroencephalography-based machine learning models for hyperacute detection of large vessel occlusion stroke.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) has shown potential as a prehospital triage instrument for anterior circulation large vessel occlusion (LVO-a) stroke. In this study, we determined the diagnostic accuracy of EEG-based machine learning algorithms for LVO-a stroke detection. Anterior circulation large vessel occlusion stroke detection machine learning models were developed using EEG data from the ELECTRA-STROKE (NCT03699397) and AI-STROKE (NCT05437237) studies. Single 2- to 3-min EEG recordings were obtained using 8 dry electrodes in adults with suspected stroke in prehospital and in-hospital settings. Patients with a clean EEG segment of ≥ 5 s (visually selected) were included and EEG symmetry features were extracted. We assessed the performance of multiple machine learning models using nested cross-validation (CV), optimising models with 3-fold CV (inner loop) and evaluating them with leave-one-out CV (outer loop). Of 1293 patients with suspected stroke, 336 (26%) were included (74% prehospital, 26% in-hospital). Median age was 72 (IQR 61-80) years, and 231 (69%) were male. Sixteen (5%) patients had LVO-a stroke, 140 (42%) non-LVO-a ischaemic stroke, 52 (15%) TIA, 13 (4%) haemorrhagic stroke and 115 (34%) a stroke mimic. Naïve Bayes achieved the highest observed area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (0.85 [95% CI, 0.77-0.93]), with a sensitivity of 69% (95% CI, 44%-86%) and specificity of 86% (95% CI, 82%-89%). Machine learning models for LVO-a stroke detection based solely on EEG showed moderately high diagnostic accuracy. These results support the potential of EEG-based LVO-a stroke detection, but improved EEG data acquisition is needed before clinical implementation can be considered.

papers.title: Distinct motor preparatory signals correlate with coarse vs fine control of self-paced action timing.
papers.abstract: Making each action at the right time is crucial for motor control. In this study, we investigated how two prominent motor preparatory processes identified in human EEG-beta-band desynchronisation and the readiness potential (RP)-might each differently relate to the time of a simple voluntary action. In our paradigm, participants learned when to act in each block of trials, based on probabilistic trial-by-trial feedback. A reward schedule reinforced a specific optimal time to act in some blocks, but allowed greater variability around the same mean action time in other blocks. We found that contralateral motor beta-band power at the beginning of each trial was higher in trials with slow actions than in those with fast actions. In contrast, contralateral beta-band power reached stereotyped low values at the time of action, regardless of waiting times. Put together, this pattern is consistent with a neural implementation of distance-to-bound for a noisy accumulation process, in which baseline motor activity starts off closer to an action-triggering bound when fast actions are required. In turn, the RP was independent of the mean waiting time before action, but its slope increased when participants developed a precise motor plan. We suggest that beta desynchronisation and the RP track distinct, complementary processes involved in the temporal control of action. While beta-power activity at trial onset is consistent with a strategic adjustment of motor preparation to match the required pace of action, the modulation of the RP by motor plan precision is consistent with a temporally structured input to a ramping preparatory process. Simulations suggest that acting at the right time may involve increasing the strength of the input to this accumulator, which can drive the decision variable to drift towards the decision bound.

papers.title: Developmental interactions between oscillatory and spontaneous neural activity support improvements in inhibitory control from adolescence into adulthood
papers.abstract: Adolescence is a critical period of development marked by improvements in cognitive control driven by maturation of executive brain systems. Neural mechanisms supporting inhibitory control (the ability to suppress a prepotent response in favor of generating a goal-directed response) mature into adulthood in parallel with refinements in frequency-specific neural oscillations and broadband spontaneous activity, supporting more accurate and reliable performance on response inhibition tasks, such as the antisaccade oculomotor task. Prior work has established that the maturation of neural circuitry contributes to age-related decreases in spontaneous activity, supporting higher-fidelity transmission of task-relevant activity, such as frequency-specific neural oscillations, which are crucial for antisaccade performance. Using longitudinal electroencephalography (EEG) data from 146 participants (72 F, ages 10-34, 253 total sessions) collected while participants performed an antisaccade task, we sought to understand the interplay between frontal oscillatory and spontaneous activity during cognitive processing and how it supports developmental improvements in inhibitory control. We found that spontaneous activity decreased developmentally during the preparation of an inhibitory response, and that this was associated with reduced trial-to-trial variability in response latency, indicating that reductions in spontaneous activity may increase the reliability of inhibitory control processing. Furthermore, performance-related decreases in broadband spontaneous activity were associated with the suppression of preparatory high-beta oscillations in an age-dependent manner, such that this relationship became more pronounced through development. Together, these results illustrate how developmental enhancements in the coordination of frequency-specific oscillations and spontaneous activity during inhibitory response preparation support developmental improvements in inhibitory control, providing a potential mechanism through which inhibitory control becomes more accurate and reliable from adolescence into adulthood.

Spontaneous activity decreased with development and was linked to lower trial-to-trial latency variability, while age-dependent suppression of preparatory high-beta oscillations became more pronounced with development.

papers.title: CEP-MI: a novel cue-execution dual-stage motor imagery paradigm with PGCANet decoding architecture.
papers.abstract: Motor imagery-based brain-computer interface (MI-BCI) holds great potential in neurorehabilitation and motor assistance. Data quality and motor intention decoding effectiveness are closely associated with participants' engagement. However, previous MI tasks ignored active engagement regulation, and neural mechanisms underlying the transition from motor imagery to execution remain unclear, with limited relevant research. Conventional separate-trial designs cannot capture continuous brain dynamics from imagery to execution and cannot objectively evaluate subject engagement, which hinders mechanism exploration and stable decoding. To address these paradigm-related limitations, a novel cue-execution MI paradigm (CEP-MI) with countdown anchors was designed to quantify engagement. Motor execution sessions were added post-imagery to reveal neural differences during the transition and identify movement-related brain activities. Meanwhile, to boost MI-EEG decoding performance, a collaborative decoding architecture (PGCANet) integrating prior guidance and channel awareness was proposed, with dual branches and consistency constraint loss for decision fusion. CEP-MI effectively quantifies participant engagement, and PGCANet achieves superior decoding performance compared to traditional algorithms and advanced models, with the optimal average accuracy reaching 85.77% in binary classification and 82.47% in quadruple classification. Targeting the above-mentioned research gaps, the CEP-MI paradigm provides valuable insights into the imagery-execution transition mechanism. PGCANet enhances MI decoding accuracy via multi-branch collaboration, laying a foundation for MI-BCI's clinical application in neurorehabilitation. This study introduces a novel paradigm and collaborative architecture that significantly advance MI-BCI decoding accuracy and engagement quantification, and helps to promote its clinical application in neurorehabilitation.

papers.title: Human iEEG recordings during audiovisual speech violations support and extend predictive routing models.
papers.abstract: Rather than constantly reconstructing the world solely through sensory input, predictive processing theories posit that the brain utilizes predictions maintained as internal representations to guide sensory processing. An emerging model, predictive routing, proposes that an interplay between neuronal gamma (40-150 Hz) and alpha-beta (10-30 Hz) rhythms implements a dynamic mechanism for predictive processing. Namely, predictions enhance alpha-beta oscillations that suppress gamma activity during the processing of predicted inputs. While this model is supported by animal studies, its validity has not been fully explored within the human brain. The present study addresses this by leveraging human intracranial EEG (iEEG) recordings across superior temporal and prefrontal/premotor areas of seven presurgical epilepsy patients during an audiovisual speech paradigm. We calculated iEEG power in the theta, alpha-beta, and high gamma bands during simple auditory deviance, multisensory integration, and a condition where an incongruent visual cue (lip movements) clashed with an auditory stimulus (a syllable), creating audiovisual incongruence that can elicit the McGurk illusion. Results revealed increased high-gamma and decreased alpha-beta power in the superior temporal cortex in response to auditory deviance and the McGurk condition, while frontal areas, despite reflecting a similar decrease in alpha-beta power, did not present this high gamma prediction error signal. Instead, the theta band revealed a strong prediction error signal in the McGurk condition, consistent with theories on the role of theta in reorganizing cortical networks. These results both support and extend existing predictive routing models for human-specific forms of predictive processing.

papers.title: Developmental trajectories of pain empathy: evidence from drift diffusion modeling and EEG time-frequency analysis.
papers.abstract: Pain empathy develops from childhood into adulthood, but the cognitive and neural processes that support this development remain incompletely understood. The present study analyzed behavioral and electroencephalography (EEG) data from 120 participants (children, adolescents, and adults) who completed an Attention-to-Pain-Cue (A-P) task and an Attention-to-Non-Pain-Cue (A-N) task with painful and non-painful limb images. A hierarchical drift-diffusion model (HDDM) was used to characterize latent decision processes, and EEG time-frequency analyses were used to examine alpha- and beta-band event-related desynchronization (ERD). Across alternative DDM specifications, children showed lower drift rates, wider decision boundaries when averaged across image types, and longer non-decision times than older participants, which could be interpreted as differences in domain-general decision dynamics within pain-related task contexts. The EEG results showed age-related differences in alpha- and beta-band ERD, with reduced neural differentiation between painful and non-painful stimuli in children when pain cues were task-irrelevant. Together, these findings suggest that pain-related processing across development is shaped by both general maturation of decision processes and the increasing ability to maintain neural sensitivity to pain cues under changing attentional demands.

papers.title: Structural and EEG Motor Networks Distinguish Level of Motor Impairment After Stroke.
papers.abstract: The objective of this study was to determine how structural and EEG-based functional connectivity jointly distinguish levels of motor impairment after stroke. We estimated patient-specific (1) structural connectivity using MRI-derived lesion models and (2) functional connectivity using source-localized EEG, guided by each patient's structural connectome. Analyses focused on the brainstem and three motor-related cortical regions bilaterally: primary motor cortex (M1), dorsal premotor cortex (PMd), and supplementary motor cortex (SMA). Network analysis metrics (degree centrality, average efficiency, betweenness centrality) were applied to structural and functional data, contrasting motor networks between patients with high (H) and low (L) upper extremity motor function. Structural disconnection of the brainstem from M1 and PMd carried the highest probability of low motor status. All network measures were elevated in the H group compared to the L group across motor-related regions, indicating a globally strengthened motor network organization associated with better motor function. Functional connectivity revealed convergent but distinct patterns. In the delta band (1-3 Hz), ipsilesional motor regions showed stronger connectivity in the H group. In the beta band (14-29 Hz), contralesional motor regions demonstrated enhanced connectivity in H patients, consistent with prior evidence that contralesional motor regions may contribute to motor function after ipsilesional injury. We also introduced a novel metric, motor betweenness centrality, to quantify the role of nonmotor regions in rerouting motor-related communication. Almost all new hubs identified structurally were associated with lower motor status, suggesting less efficient network organization in more impaired patients. Thus, preservation of direct motor pathways supports better motor status, while reliance on alternative, less efficient routes correlates with worse outcomes. By contrast, EEG routing revealed that H patients recruited proximal cortical hubs, while L patients relied on distant, inefficient ones, highlighting functional network organization not evident in the structural analysis. These patterns suggest that more local network organization, rather than more distributed rerouting, is associated with better motor status within the motor system. In summary, multimodal network properties reliably identified key motor ROIs predictive of motor status. This concordance suggests that EEG-based metrics, particularly delta- and beta-band connectivity, are associated with lesion-derived structural disruption and complementary features of motor-network organization. Structural connectivity damage within motor circuits defines the extent of network disruption associated with motor impairment, while EEG functional connectivity provides complementary information about network organization measured at the time of assessment. Together, these measures characterize different aspects of motor network integrity after stroke.

papers.title: Respiratory phase orchestrates human olfactory cortical dynamics.
papers.abstract: Olfaction is fundamental to perception, memory, and emotion, yet the neural basis of human odor processing remains poorly understood. We demonstrate that odor-evoked brain activity is organized by respiratory phase-not absolute time-revealing that natural breathing structures olfactory cortical dynamics. Using simultaneous nasal respiration and electroencephalography recordings in [Formula: see text] participants, we delivered naturalistic odors (peppermint, oregano, and grapefruit) synchronized to individual breathing cycles. Odor presentation elicited respiratory phase-locked event-related spectral perturbations (RPL-ERSPs) in frontal and temporal regions, emerging during the first breath after stimulus onset. The most discriminative neural signatures were theta-band activity during inhalation and alpha-band activity during exhalation, patterns that were obscured in traditional time-locked analyses due to natural variability in breath duration. Leave-one-subject-out cross-validation of RPL-ERSPs achieved reliable odor detection (peppermint: AUC [Formula: see text] 0.79; oregano: AUC [Formula: see text] 0.67; grapefruit: AUC [Formula: see text] 0.62), establishing that phase-locked features generalize across individuals. To connect neural responses to perceptual experience without relying on odor naming-which can be disproportionately impaired in some populations-we quantified odor recognition using free-response descriptions scored with a semantic-similarity approach. Behavioral recognition strength paralleled the neural decoding hierarchy across odors, establishing the perceptual validity of RPL-ERSPs. RPL-ERSPs revealed rapid habituation, with decoding performance declining over repeated presentations, due to selective degradation of the most informative phase-locked features. These findings establish respiratory rhythm as a temporal scaffold for human olfactory cortical processing, positioning RPL-ERSPs as a sensitive, task-free approach for assessing olfactory function. We provide an open-source, respiration-synchronized olfactometer design to enable replication and adoption.

papers.title: Opposing effects of childhood abuse and neglect on neural performance monitoring.
papers.abstract: The dimensional model of adversity proposes that threat (abuse) and deprivation (neglect) exert distinct effects on neurocognitive development. We tested whether these dimensions show opposing associations with neural indices of performance monitoring in a sample of 782 young adults from the CoScience EEG-Personality Project. Participants completed the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire alongside an Eriksen flanker task while electroencephalography was recorded. Performance monitoring was indexed by the error-related negativity and frontal midline theta activity. Consistent with preregistered hypotheses, abuse and neglect showed opposing associations with both neural measures. Higher abuse was associated with enhanced error-related negativity but not theta power, whereas higher neglect was associated with attenuated error-related negativity and reduced theta power. Exploratory analyses indicated that these associations were moderated by sex, with stronger effects observed in males. These findings are consistent with the distinction between threat- and deprivation-related adversity and suggest that different forms of childhood adversity may be linked to variation in neurocognitive processes underlying cognitive control. However, the cross-sectional and retrospective nature of the measures limits causal inference and may introduce reporting biases.

papers.title: Spectral power and functional connectivity of resting EEG in people exposed to armed conflict and controls.
papers.abstract: Exposure to armed conflict can leave persistent effects on mental health, yet its neurophysiological correlates remain poorly characterized, particularly in populations exposed to prolonged violence outside narrowly defined post traumatic stress disorder samples. Here we examined resting state electroencephalographic activity in 122 Colombian adults, including 74 participants exposed to armed conflict and 48 controls. Eyes closed EEG was analysed for 240 seconds per participant. We quantified absolute and relative spectral power across delta, theta, alpha and beta bands and regional functional connectivity using weighted phase lag index in theta, alpha and beta. Group comparisons were adjusted for age, education, sex and assessment year, with correction across 78 EEG contrasts. Median occipital and global alpha power was lower in exposed participants, although adjusted estimates were close to the null and confidence intervals were broad. Temporal theta relative power was lower in exposed participants at nominal significance; the contrast did not retain statistical significance after Holm correction. No spectral power or regional connectivity contrast met the adjusted significance threshold. Exploratory associations between EEG measures and MoCA performance were modest among participants without scoring flags. These findings characterize resting EEG in a population shaped by prolonged violence and displacement. The confidence intervals leave the magnitude and direction of several group differences uncertain, while the observed alpha and theta patterns identify questions for larger studies integrating more detailed exposure and cognitive measures.

papers.title: Intranasal CBT101 demonstrates favorable safety and neurophysiological evidence of central activity in healthy male volunteers.
papers.abstract: CBT101 is a creatine prodrug under development for disorders driven by impaired neuronal energy homeostasis, with initial development focused on creatine transporter deficiency and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. This first-in-human study aimed to assess the safety and tolerability of single and repeated ascending intranasal doses of CBT101 in healthy male volunteers and explored neurophysiological evidence of central pharmacodynamic activity using quantitative EEG (qEEG) and event-related potentials (ERPs). This was a randomized, double-blind, single-center, placebo-controlled phase 1 trial including single ascending dose (SAD) and multiple ascending dose (MAD) parts. Forty-eight healthy male volunteers were randomized 3:1 to CBT101 or placebo. CBT101 was administered intranasally at 4.2, 8.4, or 12.6 mg in the SAD part and at 4.2, 8.4, or 12.6 mg/day for 14 days in the MAD part. The primary objective was safety and tolerability. Secondary analyses assessed quantitative EEG (qEEG) and event-related potentials (ERPs) as pharmacodynamic evaluations. No serious or severe treatment-emergent adverse events occurred, no dose-limiting toxicity was observed, and no clinically relevant safety findings were reported. As expected, plasma CBT101 concentrations were below the limit of quantification in all analyzed samples. qEEG analyses identified an acute post-dose increase in relative beta activity after single dosing. After repeated dosing, the qEEG profile evolved toward a more sustained pattern characterized by beta-1 modulation and early gamma-band changes. ERP/P300 analyses showed a transient decrease in P300 latency, with no statistically significant change in P300 amplitude. Intranasal CBT101 was safe and well tolerated across the evaluated SAD and MAD dose ranges in healthy male volunteers. Convergent qEEG and ERP findings provided early neurophysiological evidence of central pharmacodynamic engagement. These findings support continued clinical development of CBT101 for disorders associated with impaired neuronal energy homeostasis. ClinicalTrials.gov, identifier: NCT07050316.

papers.title: Scalable hardware and software for high-density, multi-regional electrophysiology in non-human primates.
papers.abstract: Understanding how distributed neural circuits generate complex behaviors requires long-duration recordings from populations of individual neurons across multiple brain regions. High-density Neuropixels probes have revolutionized rodent systems neuroscience. Extending these capabilities to non-human primates (NHPs) for chronic, multi-regional recordings requires compact, implantable microdrive hardware and reliable automated spike-sorting software. NHPs provide access to complex and flexible behaviors that are difficult to study in other model systems. Extending the Neuropixels revolution to NHPs therefore depends on integrating hardware and software for long-duration, multi-regional recordings. Here, we present a scalable hardware-software platform co-designed for high-density neural data acquisition and reliable single-unit identification in NHPs. The Multi-regional Implantable NeuroDrive (MIND) is a lightweight, implantable microdrive that provides stable recordings from multiple independently positioned Neuropixels probes and is designed to support chronic, ambulatory, head-free recordings. We paired MIND with UnitAssay, an automated post-sorting curation framework that identifies and curates characteristic spike-sorting errors with minimal computational cost. Together, MIND and UnitAssay provide an integrated platform for implanted, multi-regional recordings in NHPs performing complex and naturalistic behaviors. We tested MIND and UnitAssay across parietal, prefrontal, and motor cortices in rhesus macaques performing reaching and eye-movement tasks. MIND enabled stable multi-probe recordings across cortical regions and durations. UnitAssay enabled automated curation of large-scale spike-sorting output and improved reliable single-unit identification relative to Kilosort 4 labels and standard SpikeInterface quality control. Together, MIND and UnitAssay provide a scalable solution for high-density, multi-regional, long-duration electrophysiology in NHPs.

papers.title: Resting-State EEG Spectral Power in Young Adults With Generalized Anxiety Disorder and Self-Reported Habitual Short Sleep: A Case-Control Study.
papers.abstract: Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) and insufficient sleep frequently co-occur during early adulthood, yet resting-state electroencephalographic (EEG) evidence in this population remains limited. The present study aimed to characterize resting-state EEG spectral power in young adults with GAD who also reported habitual short sleep, compared with healthy controls. This exploratory case-control study included 56 university students: 28 participants with GAD and self-reported habitual short sleep and 28 healthy controls. Resting-state EEG spectral power was quantified in the delta, theta, alpha, and beta bands. We retained unadjusted group comparisons for description and fitted age- and sex-adjusted linear models for the primary inferential interpretation. Channel-wise models likewise included group, age, and sex, with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction across the 30 channels within each frequency band. After adjustment for age and sex, group coefficients remained positive for delta (2.51, 95% CI: 0.20 to 4.82), theta (2.52, 95% CI: 0.29 to 4.74), alpha (2.46, 95% CI: -0.12 to 5.03), and beta power (2.14, 95% CI: 0.13 to 4.15), but none met the FDR threshold (adjusted FDR p = 0.0501, 0.0501, 0.0608, and 0.0501, respectively). In unadjusted analyses, delta, theta, and beta differences survived FDR correction (FDR p = 0.0480 for each), whereas alpha did not (FDR p = 0.0553). In adjusted channel-wise analyses, 26 channel-by-band comparisons across 15 channels survived within-band FDR correction; all occurred in delta or theta and were concentrated over posterior and centroparietal electrodes. Whole-scalp estimates were directionally higher in the GAD plus habitual short-sleep group, but no age- and sex-adjusted frequency-band comparison survived FDR correction. Adjusted exploratory channel-wise findings indicated a posterior and centroparietal concentration in delta and theta power. These estimates remain preliminary and do not permit attribution to GAD, habitual short sleep, or their interaction.

papers.title: Electric and Magnetic Source Imaging in Epilepsy: Anatomical Insights from Realistic Simulations
papers.abstract: Neurosurgery is an effective treatment for drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE), but its success depends on the accurate delineation of the epileptogenic focus, approximated noninvasively by electric and magnetic source imaging (ESI/MSI) of high-density electroencephalography (HD-EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG). These modalities have distinct sensitivity profiles; consequently, epileptiform activity detected by one modality may remain undetected by the other. However, the implications of these differences for spike detectability and localization accuracy, and the added value of combined electromagnetic source imaging (EMSI), remain insufficiently characterized under clinically realistic conditions. Here, we characterize HD-EEG and MEG sensitivity profiles and compare ESI, MSI, and EMSI, using realistic simulations with known ground truth. We generated HD-EEG and MEG datasets from cortical, insular, and hippocampal sources across multiple orientations, activated using patient-derived intracranial EEG spike waveforms. Spike sensitivity and localization accuracy were evaluated using dipole scanning, dynamic statistical parametric mapping (dSPM), and linearly constrained minimum variance (LCMV). EEG demonstrated higher spike detection rates and sensitivity for radially cortical sources at gyral crowns and sulcal bottoms (p<0.001), while MEG detected more spikes from tangential cortical sources along sulcal walls (p<0.001). MSI localized tangential sources more accurately than ESI across all methods (p<0.001), while dipole scanning outperformed dSPM and LCMV for cortical and insular sources (p<0.001). EMSI outperformed ESI (p<0.001) but did not improve localization over MSI. These findings suggest that complementary anatomical sensitivities of HD-EEG and MEG may improve epileptogenic source characterization, supporting simultaneous acquisition during the presurgical evaluation of patients with DRE.

papers.title: Different modes of stimulation at the Neiguan acupoint (PC6) regulate different EEG microstates under VR immersion conditions.
papers.abstract: Acupuncture at the Neiguan acupoint (PC6) alleviates postoperative and chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting. Nevertheless, the central regulatory effects of PC6 stimulation on virtual reality motion sickness (VRMS), a form of physiological vertigo triggered by visual-vestibular sensory conflict, and the corresponding alterations in electroencephalogram (EEG) microstate characteristics remain unclear. Using EEG microstate analysis as the primary approach, this study investigated the effects of different PC6 stimulation modalities on dynamic brain functional changes during VRMS, aiming to further elucidate the potential neural mechanisms underlying acupoint stimulation in VRMS. Participants were recruited based on their Motion Sickness Susceptibility Questionnaire scores, with a cut-off value of ≥34 used as the inclusion criterion. A total of 200 healthy participants were enrolled and randomly assigned to four equal groups (n = 50 per group): control (32 °C), 40 °C, 44 °C, and 2-Hz transcutaneous electrical acupoint stimulation (TEAS). The experimental protocol consisted of three phases: baseline, active stimulation, and post-stimulation. All participants received a 40-min stimulation targeting the right PC6 acupoint. EEG data were continuously recorded throughout the experiment. Microstate analysis revealed that during the stimulation phase, the 2-Hz TEAS group exhibited significantly increased duration, occurrence, and coverage of microstate D compared with the control group, whereas the 40 °C group affected only the duration of microstate D. During the post-stimulation phase, compared with the control group, the 44 °C group showed a decreased duration of microstate A and significantly increased duration and coverage of microstate B, while the 2-Hz TEAS group continued to exhibit sustained effects on the duration of microstate D. The neuroelectrophysiological signatures of stimulation at PC6 in modulating VRMS are predominantly reflected in the dynamic changes of microstates A, B, and D. Thermal stimulation and low-frequency electrical stimulation engage distinct central modulatory pathways, providing a neuroelectrophysiological basis for optimizing stimulation parameters for in future studies on VRMS.

papers.title: Clinical characteristics, semiology, and comorbidity patterns in non-epileptic seizures (NES): a retrospective comparative study.
papers.abstract: Non-epileptic seizures (NES) are paroxysmal events resembling epileptic seizures but not explained by ictal activity. Differential diagnosis may be challenging, particularly because NES and epilepsy can coexist. We aimed to characterize the demographic, clinical, semiological, psychiatric, and instrumental profile of patients with NES, compare patients with NES only with patients with NES epilepsy-only, and assess the robustness of the main associations through sensitivity analyses. We conducted a retrospective observational comparative study using a clinical database from our Neurology Unit (2022-2025) including 38 patients with NES and 23 patients with epilepsy without NES. A total of 18 NES patients had comorbid epilepsy; therefore, the primary comparison included mutually exclusive groups: NES-only (n = 20) and epilepsy-only (n = 23). All NES patients were retained for descriptive analyses. Between-group comparisons used exact or non-parametric tests with Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate (BH-FDR) correction. Sensitivity analyses restricted NES-only patients to those with database-recorded video-EEG confirmation and used Firth penalized logistic regression adjusted for age and sex. Among 38 patients with NES, 94.7% had documented psychological/psychiatric comorbidity, mainly anxiety (50.0%) and depression (28.9%). Positive motor phenomena were documented in 73.7%, neurological examination inconsistency/incongruity in 85.7% of evaluable patients, and video-EEG confirmation in 73.7%. Psychological/psychiatric comorbidity was significantly more frequent in NES-only than epilepsy-only patients (90.0% vs. 13.0%; exact OR 50.40, 95% CI 7.29-670.28; BH-FDR p < 0.001), as was anxiety (45.0% vs. 4.3%; BH-FDR p = 0.014). Broad seizure-semiology domains were not significantly different after multiplicity correction. Among imaged patients, abnormal MRI findings were more frequent in epilepsy-only patients (12/18 vs. 0/10; BH-FDR p = 0.006), although MRI ascertainment differed between groups. The psychiatric-comorbidity association persisted in sensitivity analyses. NES showed substantial clinical heterogeneity and frequently coexisted with epilepsy. Psychological/psychiatric comorbidity was markedly more frequent in NES-only than epilepsy-only patients and remained robust in sensitivity analyses, although differential ascertainment limits interpretation. Broad seizure manifestations alone did not distinguish the groups after multiplicity correction. Instrumental findings should be considered descriptive rather than NES biomarkers. These findings support explicit stratification for comorbid epilepsy and standardized prospective assessment of psychiatric and semiological features.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Neurology: A Critical Narrative Review of Clinical Evidence, Translation, and Responsible Implementation.
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied to neuroimaging, electrophysiology, clinical text, and digitally measured behavior, but reported performance often exceeds the maturity of clinical evidence. We conducted a structured narrative review, informed by SANRA principles, of English-language human studies, reviews, and regulatory sources identified in PubMed/MEDLINE and IEEE Xplore from January 2022 through July 2026; older landmark studies were retained when necessary for historical or methodological context. We applied a common translational-evidence framework across six prespecified neurological domains to distinguish technical performance from external validation, prospective clinical evaluation, implementation, and demonstrated patient benefit. Evidence was appraised according to cohort representativeness, patient-level data separation, external and prospective validation, calibration, clinical comparators, regulatory status, workflow integration, and patient-level benefit. Across stroke, dementia, Parkinson disease, epilepsy, multiple sclerosis, and neuro-oncology, the strongest evidence concerns narrowly defined imaging and signal-processing tasks. A cluster-randomized stroke study demonstrated shorter thrombectomy workflow time, and several externally validated models show improved portability. In contrast, many high-accuracy classification and segmentation studies remain retrospective, single-dataset, internally validated, and uncalibrated. Multimodal learning, foundation models, federated learning, and large language models broaden capability but introduce additional risks related to dataset shift, bias, opacity, privacy, and automation. Neuro-AI should be judged by its intended clinical task and evidence maturity rather than headline accuracy. Multicenter external validation, prospective workflow evaluation, calibration, subgroup reporting, human-factors testing, and post-deployment surveillance are prerequisites for safe and equitable clinical use.

papers.title: Working memory supports cognitive control by orchestrating dimension-specific modulation during late conflict resolution.
papers.abstract: Working memory plays a central role in cognitive control, yet how it shapes target- and distractor-related processing over time remains unclear. Here, we combined a working memory load manipulation with a modified Stroop task in which distractors preceded targets. Behaviorally, we found that pre-exposure to the distractor eliminated the congruency effect, but this benefit was absent under high load. This pattern suggests that the benefit of advance distractor presentation is sensitive to concurrent working-memory demands. Electrophysiologically, the distractor-locked lateralized readiness potential (LRP) indicated that working-memory load altered distractor-related response activation before target onset. After target onset, load-related modulation emerged during late conflict resolution, as indexed by the sustained potential (SP), whereas earlier intervals associated with attentional selection (posterior N2) and conflict monitoring (N450) did not show load-dependent modulation. Time-frequency decoding and representational similarity analysis further revealed distinct spectro-temporal profiles of target- and distractor-related processing: target-related coding emerged earlier in the theta band (540-780 ms), consistent with stimulus-response mapping, whereas distractor-related coding emerged later in the mu-beta band (870-1180 ms), consistent with response-related regulation. These findings highlight dimension- and stage-specific patterns of working-memory modulation during conflict resolution.

papers.title: Disrupted cortical signatures of response inhibition in Parkinson's disease revealed by TMS-EEG.
papers.abstract: Inhibitory control deficits are a hallmark of Parkinson's disease (PD), particularly in patients with L-DOPA-induced dyskinesias (LID), but the cortical mechanisms underlying impaired inhibition remain poorly understood. We used transcranial magnetic stimulation and electroencephalography (TMS-EEG) to investigate cortical dynamics during a Go/NoGo task in PD patients with and without LID, compared with healthy volunteers. Thirty-six PD patients (18 LID-PD, 18 nLID-PD) and 20 healthy volunteers performed a Go/NoGo task during TMS-EEG, which assessed functional connectivity between the supplementary motor area (SMA) and primary motor cortex (M1), and cortical reactivity through TMS-evoked potentials. Healthy volunteers exhibited task-dependent modulation of SMA-M1 connectivity, with increased theta-band coupling during NoGo trials and gamma-band coupling during Go trials; this pattern was absent in both PD groups, particularly in those with dyskinesias. TMS-evoked potentials revealed enhanced N100 responses during NoGo trials in healthy volunteers, reduced in non-dyskinetic patients and absent in dyskinetic ones. SMA-M1 gamma connectivity correlated with motor performance and clinical severity. During post-TMS epochs, healthy volunteers showed context-dependent alpha/beta modulation that was disrupted in PD patients. SMA-M1 communication and cortical inhibitory processing are impaired in PD, especially in patients with dyskinesias. SMA dysfunction may represent a biomarker and therapeutic target for inhibitory deficits in PD.

papers.title: Real-world efficacy and safety profile of sulthiame treatment in drug-resistant childhood epilepsy.
papers.abstract: Sulthiame (STM) is a potent carbonic anhydrase inhibitor primarily used in focal epilepsy syndromes; however, clinical data regarding its efficacy and safety in broader drug-resistant childhood epilepsy remain limited. This study aimed to evaluate the clinical efficacy, electroencephalographic response, and safety profile of STM in a cohort of pediatric patients with drug-resistant epilepsy. A retrospective medical chart review was conducted for patients under 18 years of age treated with STM at a tertiary pediatric neurology clinic between 2011 and 2024. Data including demographic characteristics, etiology, seizure semiology, epilepsy syndromes, treatment duration, and dosage were analyzed. Electroencephalographic (EEG) findings were assessed using EEG recordings obtained within 1-3 months after initiation of sulthiame therapy. Seizure frequency outcomes were assessed by comparing baseline seizure frequency with seizure frequency at the final available clinical follow-up. Sixty-one patients (55.7% female; median seizure onset: 14 months) were included. A structural etiology was identified in 50.8% of patients, and 62.3% had a well-defined epilepsy syndrome. At the final available clinical follow-up, 41% (n = 25) of patients achieved complete seizure freedom, while 16.4% (n = 10) showed a ≥ 50% reduction in seizure frequency. Conversely, 42.6% demonstrated a < 50% reduction. A higher number of previously failed anti-seizure medications (ASMs) was significantly associated with a poorer treatment response (p = 0.014). EEG improvement was observed in 44.3% of the cohort. Notably, focal seizure semiology was associated with favorable EEG outcomes, whereas combined semiology was linked to electroencephalographic worsening (p = 0.026). STM was generally well-tolerated; adverse effects were reported in only nine patients, with treatment discontinuation required in only two cases (3.2%). Sulthiame is an effective and well-tolerated therapeutic option for children with drug-resistant epilepsy, particularly those with focal semiology. Our findings suggest that a higher burden of prior ASM treatment negatively impacts response rates, highlighting the potential benefit of considering STM earlier in the treatment algorithm for specific pediatric populations.

papers.title: Neuromodulatory effects of audio-proprio-phonatory reinforcement training on subjective tinnitus, a HD-EEG study protocol.
papers.abstract: Tinnitus affects 14% of the global population, with 2% experiencing a severe form of the condition. Sound therapy using white noise emitted by hearing aids is a common intervention, supported by the phenomenon of residual inhibition observed during tinnitus assessment. This study aims to investigate whether audio-proprio-phonatory reinforcement training can improve the quality of life of patients with chronic subjective tinnitus by enabling them to listen to their own phonation, which may mask the tinnitus or induce residual inhibition. We will conduct a prospective, controlled, monocentric, 2-arm block-randomized study, stratified by the Tinnitus Handicap Inventory (THI) score, involving two groups for two sequential phases (Phase 1 and Phase 2). Fifty-six patients with tinnitus, recruited from the Ear Nose Throat (ENT) Department of Orléans University Hospital, will undergo a five-week training program, randomized into weekly remote group workshops, and daily individual sessions using specially developed videos. Training efficacy will be assessed through self-report questionnaires. The primary endpoint, the Tinnitus Handicap Inventory, will be assessed at three ENT medical visits: at inclusion, end of phase 1 and end of phase 2. Additionally, patients in both groups will regularly complete Visual Analog Scales for Tinnitus and five related questions (noise, cervical, jaw, sleep, stress-anxiety) via a secure digital platform throughout the study. High-density electroencephalograms (HD-EEG) will be performed in a blinded manner before and after Phase 1 at the Neurology Department of Orléans University Hospital. This pilot study aims to evaluate the clinical efficacy of audio-proprio-phonatory training in patients with chronic subjective tinnitus and to objectively measure its effects using HD-EEG. We will explore potential correlations between changes brain activity (such as functional brain connectivity) and clinical responses to the intervention.

papers.title: Restorative streetscapes in high-density urban tourism: environmental archetypes, visual attention, and psychophysiological responses.
papers.abstract: In high-density tourist districts, visitors are continuously exposed to the visual environments of surrounding streets, forecourts, and small public spaces before reaching an attraction, and these transitional spaces may influence short-term restorative states. Existing research has typically examined urban-scale streetscape characteristics and human responses under experimental conditions separately, with limited provision of a reproducible procedure for selecting experimental stimuli from large environmental samples. Taking the high-density urban core around Hong Kong's Victoria Harbour as a case study, this study identified 66 tourism-related sites and acquired four fixed-direction streetscape images for each site, yielding 264 images in total. A 66 × 11 objective environmental matrix was constructed from five GIS-based environmental indicators and six streetscape-image proxy indicators. Principal component analysis (PCA) summarized the dominant environmental gradients, and k = 6 K-means was retained as a pragmatic six-group sampling solution aligned with the pre-specified six-scene experimental capacity rather than as a uniquely optimal or stable urban typology. Forty-six of 48 registered adults contributed 108 focal-scene exposures. After BH-FDR correction, significant differences among the six scenes were observed in perceived restorativeness, the proportion of fixations on natural areas of interest (AOIs), gaze entropy, changes in EEG alpha-minus-theta, mean EDA skin conductance level (SCL), and HRV RMSSD, whereas sustained-attention accuracy showed no significant scene effect. Oil Street Art Space exhibited the highest perceived restorativeness (5.69/7), the highest proportion of fixations on natural AOIs (51.4%), and the largest increases in EEG (+2.68) and HRV RMSSD (+11.37 ms), while Western Market showed the lowest restorativeness (4.17/7), the lowest natural-AOI fixation share (31.2%), and the smallest EEG increase (+1.93). Sensitivity analyses showed no evidence of scene-by-order interaction for perceived restorativeness, natural-AOI fixation, gaze entropy, or SART accuracy, but EEG, EDA, and HRV were more order-sensitive; the principal subjective, attentional, EEG, and HRV contrasts remained evident when analysis was restricted to each participant's earliest focal-scene exposure. These findings therefore support scene-configuration contrasts under short-term static visual exposure. Building on the environmental structure of the 66 sites and the multimodal responses to the six experimental scenes, the study further proposes an archetype-calibrated framework for mapping restorative potential in high-density tourist streetscapes, providing a spatial basis for identifying restorative opportunity nodes and priority intervention areas.

papers.title: Large Vision-Language Models for Pediatric Motor Tic Detection: Case-Control Diagnostic Study.
papers.abstract: Clinical diagnosis of tic disorders (TDs) is often delayed by fluctuating symptoms and the subjective nature of assessments. While automated methods have been proposed to bridge this gap, traditional machine learning models frequently lack robustness in unconstrained environments and fail to capture the complex, multisite tics characteristic of severe TDs. This study aimed to develop and evaluate a fine-tuned large vision-language model framework for the automated, interpretable detection of pediatric motor tics, addressing the clinical need for objective and efficient symptom assessment in unconstrained environments. In this multicenter study, 168 pediatric participants (n=83, 49.4% with TDs and n=85, 50.6% healthy controls) underwent 12-hour continuous video-electroencephalography monitoring. We fine-tuned the Qwen3-VL-8B model using 3- to 5-minute video segments via low-rank adaptation. The framework used chain-of-thought prompting to generate both binary classifications and textual justifications. A strict patient-wise split ensured zero identity overlap between training and test sets. Diagnostic precision was evaluated using 95% CIs calculated with the Clopper-Pearson exact method. In total, 168 pediatric participants (age: mean 8.3, SD 2.3 years) were enrolled, providing 559 expert-validated video segments for analysis. On the independent test set (n=55), the framework achieved 89.1% (49/55; 95% CI 77.8%-95.9%) accuracy and an area under the curve of 0.950 (95% CI 0.892-1.000), significantly outperforming the landmark-based deep neural network (accuracy 74.1%; P=.004); recall reached 100% (25/25 positive episodes; 95% CI 86.3%-100.0%). Model-generated justifications showed substantial agreement with expert annotations (κ=0.784, 95% CI 0.625-0.943; P<.001). These findings suggest that a vision-language model framework can capture clinically relevant tic features beyond conventional geometric descriptors. By combining high sensitivity (recall) with text-based diagnostic justifications aligned with clinical severity dimensions (eg, frequency and intensity), the approach may support automated video review and preliminary symptom quantification in controlled monitoring settings.

papers.title: Assessing the Effectiveness, Engagement, and Acceptability of a Smartwatch Healthy Lifestyle Intervention for Cognitive Enhancement in Healthy Adults: Mixed Methods Electroencephalography Protocol.
papers.abstract: Wearable technologies are rapidly transforming the health care landscape by enabling the tracking of real-time physiological and behavioral data used in healthy lifestyle interventions. Despite their widespread adoption in the consumer market, scientific validation of their impact on the brain remains limited, and factors influencing effects on cognition and adherence are not fully understood. This gap is critical, as consumers, health care providers, and researchers depend on these data to unlock the potential of wearables for cognitive support. We aim to assess the effectiveness, engagement, and acceptability of a commercially available smartwatch healthy lifestyle intervention on cognitive enhancement in healthy adults, using a convergent parallel mixed methods design. We seek to provide a comprehensive, replicable methodological framework to evaluate wearable technology interventions targeting cognitive enhancement in healthy adults. Healthy adults aged 18 to 40 years with a sedentary lifestyle (N=72) interested in participating in a healthy lifestyle intervention will be recruited in the Vancouver Metropolitan Area, BC, Canada. Participants will be randomly assigned into an intervention group using an Apple Watch or a control group following standard physical activity guidelines without an Apple Watch for a period of 4 weeks. Effectiveness will be evaluated through (1) cognitive function (primary outcome)-executive function, specifically inhibitory control, via electroencephalogram-based event-related potentials (N2/P3) during a go/no-go task; (2) resting-state brain activity via electroencephalogram spectral power; (3) behavioral performance (reaction time and accuracy); (4) perceived health (36-item Short Form Health Survey); and (5) qualitative analysis of factors affecting the intervention's effectiveness. Engagement will be assessed through goal completion metrics and qualitative analysis of barriers, facilitators, and usage patterns. Acceptability will be assessed through System Usability Scale scores and qualitative analysis of factors affecting usability, satisfaction, and user preferences. This design integrates assessments before, during, and after intervention. Qualitative assessments will include weekly check-ins and semistructured interviews to obtain a comprehensive understanding of factors influencing the effectiveness, engagement, and acceptability of the intervention. Exploratory outcomes include descriptions of possible interactions between the 3 constructs and comparison of smartwatch-tracked vs self-reported goal completion. The study received funding from the AGE-WELL Network Centres of Excellence (April 2020-March 2023) and was approved by the Simon Fraser University Research Ethics Board. Enrollment for the study is ongoing. As of October 2026, data have been collected from 48 participants and are currently being processed and analyzed. The first results are expected to be published in 2027. This study outlines a foundational framework for evaluating the effectiveness, engagement, and acceptability of wearable health interventions targeting cognitive enhancement in healthy adults. Furthermore, our mixed methods approach with randomized controlled comparison is expected to inform the design and development of effective, engaging, and friendly wearable brain health technologies.

papers.title: Cooperative processing of visual threat across collicular pathways.
papers.abstract: Rapid defensive actions require the transformation of sensory cues into appropriate motor responses. The superior colliculus is central to this transformation, containing defined cell-types that form parallel output pathways linking visual inputs to distinct behaviors. However, whether these pathways act independently or cooperate remains unclear. Here we combine cell-type-specific inhibition, large-scale electrophysiology, and functional ultrasound imaging to determine how these pathways contribute to visually evoked defensive behaviors. Inhibiting either narrow-field or wide-field neurons impaired escape to overhead visual threats, demonstrating that both pathways contribute to escape. Recordings from downstream targets revealed a compact representation in the deeper layers of the superior colliculus that selectively distinguished visual stimuli associated with escape, whereas the lateral posterior thalamus contained a broader representation of visual stimuli. The representation of visual threat in the deeper layers of the superior colliculus predicted escape initiation and vigor in freely moving animals. Across the brain, functional ultrasound imaging showed that visual stimuli recruited distinct patterns of activity that could not be explained by response magnitude alone or by the contribution of single cell-types. Together, these results reveal a cooperative circuit architecture in which parallel pathways carry distinct but complementary signals that jointly support visually evoked escape.

papers.title: The SIK1-NR4A2 axis: a core driver of epilepsy identified by integrated machine learning and experimental validation.
papers.abstract: Epilepsy remains a major clinical challenge, suggesting that mechanisms beyond the classical excitation-inhibition imbalance contribute to epilepsy. The Liver kinase B1 (LKB1) signaling pathway coordinates energy homeostasis and cell survival, but its key downstream effectors in epilepsy remain largely unknown. We integrated machine learning screening of LKB1 pathway genes using public Gene Expression Omnibus datasets (GSE143272) with in vivo and in vitro experimental validation. A PTZ-induced status epilepticus rat model, AAV-mediated gene knockdown/overexpression, lentiviral transfection of primary hippocampal neurons, Electroencephalography recording, whole-cell patch-clamp recording, and Western blot analysis were employed to investigate the functional role and molecular mechanisms of candidate genes. Machine learning identified SIK1 (salt-inducible kinase 1) as the top-ranked epilepsy risk gene within the LKB1 pathway. SIK1 expression was significantly upregulated in the hippocampus of SE rats. AAV-mediated SIK1 knockdown prolonged seizure latency and reduced seizure duration, while SIK1 overexpression exacerbated seizure severity. Mechanistically, through PPI network analysis and mediation analysis, we identified NR4A2 as a downstream effector of SIK1. SIK1 negatively regulated NR4A2 expression: SIK1 knockdown increased NR4A2, whereas SIK1 overexpression decreased NR4A2. Rescue experiments showed that co-overexpression of SIK1 and NR4A2 reversed the pro-epileptic effect of SIK1 alone. Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings demonstrated that SIK1 knockdown or NR4A2 overexpression restored action potential amplitude to near-normal levels in magnesium-free-treated neurons. SIK1 negatively regulates NR4A2, and restoring NR4A2 expression counteracts SIK1-induced neuronal hyperexcitability. These findings suggest that targeting the SIK1-NR4A2 axis may represent a potential therapeutic strategy for epilepsy.

papers.title: A subtype-specific gene regulatory program controls differential circuit integration of deep CA3 pyramidal neurons
papers.abstract: How closely related neuronal subtypes integrate into different circuits remains poorly understood. Deep and superficial hippocampal CA3 pyramidal neurons (PNs) differ in intrinsic firing and mossy fiber (MF) input at specialized postsynaptic structures termed thorny excrescences (TEs). Combining developmental single-nucleus multiomics with genetic targeting, morphological analysis and electrophysiology, we identify the transcription factor ST18 as a regulator of deep CA3 subtype identity. ST18 marks sparsely thorny and burst-firing neurons, and gene regulatory analyses predict that it represses a superficial-associated program involved in dendritic spine development, synaptic organization, and electrophysiological properties. Postnatal ST18 loss shifts the transcriptional and chromatin landscape of deep CA3 PNs toward a superficial-like state. These molecular changes are accompanied by increased TE elaboration approaching superficial levels, enhanced excitatory synaptic activity, and reduced burst-firing. Together, these findings identify ST18-dependent restriction of an alternative subtype program as a mechanism linking molecular identity to distinct input connectivity patterns and intrinsic firing properties during postnatal circuit maturation.

papers.title: A mechanistic classification of GNAO1 mutations links Gβγ sequestration to hyperkinetic disease and treatment response.
papers.abstract: Gα o is the most prevalent G protein α subunit in the brain and is critical for signal transduction through G protein-coupled receptors. Mutations in the gene encoding Gα o ( GNAO1 ) cause a rare neurodevelopmental disorder with involuntary movements (NEDIM) and, in some patients, developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE). Here, we integrate human genetic analysis with cellular assays to define mechanistic classes of GNAO1 mutations and in vivo approaches to evaluate therapeutic strategies. We grouped variants into two functional categories: those predicted to sequester Gβγ and those with reduced Gα o expression and therefore increased Gβγ signaling. Analysis of patient data revealed that mutations predicted to impair Gβγ release are significantly associated with NEDIM. Using the GNAO1 R209H/+ mouse as a model of NEDIM, we evaluated two small molecules: caffeine, a nonselective adenosine receptor antagonist, and gallein, a selective modulator of Gβγ-effector interactions. Both compounds significantly reduced hyperlocomotion in the open field test. Whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiology revealed sex- and cell type-specific hyperexcitability in spiny projection neurons within the dorsolateral striatum of GNAO1 R209H/+ mice. Together, these findings implicate dysfunction of dorsolateral striatal pathways in GNAO1-related disorder and suggest that mechanistic understanding of disease variants can guide targeted therapeutic strategies.

papers.title: Right heart remodeling in Sugen/hypoxia rat model of severe pulmonary hypertension.
papers.abstract: Pulmonary hypertension (PH) directly impacts the right heart through pressure overload. Unlike well-characterized remodeling of the left ventricle in systemic hypertension, PH-induced changes in the right heart are less understood. Here, we investigate chamber-specific alterations in the right atrium (RA) and right ventricle (RV) in a rat model of PH. PH was induced in 6-week-old male Wistar rats using Sugen/hypoxia (SuHx) treatment. Right heart pressure overload was confirmed by catheterization. Cardiac remodeling was characterized by using confocal microscopy, micro-CT, optical mapping, and proteomic mass spectrometry. The increase in right-heart mass was predominantly attributable to cardiomyocyte hypertrophy, with concomitant extracellular-matrix remodeling. Hypertrophy was associated with significantly elevated right heart pressures after SuHx treatment, further progressing during the subsequent normoxia. At the end of the PH protocol, electrophysiology analysis showed significant prolongation of the action potential in both the RA and RV. Proteomic analysis revealed pronounced alterations in the RV, with substantial overlap with the RA and LV, and more upregulated than downregulated proteins. GO analysis indicated increased expression of sarcomeric and fibrillar proteins and reduced expression of proteins related to oxidative energy production. In conclusion, myocardial remodeling in PH is based on cardiomyocyte hypertrophy rather than cell proliferation. Electrophysiological changes along with increased pressure in the right atrium might contribute to phenotype progression. Changes in proteome show commonalities and differences in RA and RV pressure-induced pathways that that warrant therapeutic exploration.

papers.title: Rapidly progressive cognitive decline and drug-induced encephalopathy secondary to teprotumumab for thyroid eye disease: a case report and narrative literature review.
papers.abstract: Teprotumumab, a fully human monoclonal antibody targeting insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor (IGF-1R), is an approved targeted therapy for thyroid eye disease (TED). Teprotumumab-associated encephalopathy is an extremely rare but potentially severe central nervous system adverse event, with only three cases reported globally to date. We report the first Han-Chinese patient with Graves' disease and associated TED complicated by teprotumumab-associated encephalopathy, together with a narrative review of all published cases, to raise clinicians' awareness and improve early recognition and management of this rare complication. A 56-year-old Chinese man with Graves' disease and TED developed acute progressive apathy and encephalopathy characterised by multidomain cognitive and behavioral dysfunction 20 days after the third teprotumumab infusion, with an admission MMSE score of 15. Contrast-enhanced brain MRI, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination, and autoimmune encephalitis antibody screening were unremarkable. Prolonged video-electroencephalography(VEEG) demonstrated intermittent diffuse bilateral slow-wave activity, and widespread interictal epileptiform discharges without electrographic or clinical seizures. Systematic workup excluded infectious, autoimmune, metabolic, and psychiatric encephalopathy. Treatment-emergent hyperglycemia was confirmed as a secondary aggravating factor rather than the primary cause. The patient achieved prominent neurological recovery after individualized treapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) and symptomatic management, with a Naranjo score of 6 indicating probable drug-related encephalopathy. Synthesis of all three previously published teprotumumab-associated encephalopathy cases demonstrates that neurological toxicity can develop as early as the third infusion cycle. These cases present consistent neuroimaging features with variable CSF profiles, and thyroid autoantibody elevation predominantly reflects pre-existing Graves' disease-related autoimmune background instead of directly mediating neurotoxicity. TPE generally facilitates neurological recovery but may be complicated by procedural hypersensitivity and fluctuating therapeutic responses. Notably, interictal epileptiform discharges on VEEG represent a newly identified neurophysiological manifestation of this rare adverse event. A three-hit interacting pathogenic hypothesis is proposed: impaired IGF-1R-dependent neurotrophic signalling serves as the core injury mechanism, while underlying thyroid autoimmunity and treatment-related metabolic disturbance act as susceptibility-modifying factors. This case expands the ethnic and clinical spectrum of teprotumumab-related encephalopathy. Diffuse interictal epileptiform discharges without ictal changes reflect reactive cortical hyperexcitability secondary to acute encephalopathy. Metabolic disturbance merely exacerbated neurological impairment. Limitations include single-case constraints, simultaneous multi-intervention therapy, and lack of direct intracranial mechanistic evidence. Teprotumumab-associated encephalopathy is a rare but serious adverse event. Close neurological surveillance and are essential during medication. Accumulated cases are needed to establish unified diagnostic and therapeutic criteria.
